sections.title: Know what to expect. Know how to ask. Know how to participate.
sections.subtitle: Plain-language guides to your rights, service delivery standards, local participation, and grievance redressal — written so you can act on them today.

sections.title: Everyday rights — explained simply
sections.subtitle: Pick the area that's relevant to you today. Each tab has the basics, the documents you'll need, and the office to approach.

items.label: 🏡 Land
items.title: Land & property
body: Every citizen has the right to clear title, accurate records, and transparent transactions in land and property. The Ente Bhoomi portal in Kerala is a recent example of what good land governance looks like in practice.
bullets: Your name on the land record should match your ID; mismatches can be corrected through the village office.
Every transaction (sale, mortgage, partition) creates a mutation entry — ask for it in writing.
Encumbrance certificates show whether the land has been pledged or has outstanding liabilities.

cards.title: Get a record of rights
cards.description: Visit the village office or use the state's online land records portal (e.g., Ente Bhoomi in Kerala).

cards.title: Check encumbrances
cards.description: Ask for an encumbrance certificate before buying — it lists past loans and liens.

cards.title: Correct an error
cards.description: Apply for mutation correction at the village office. Bring supporting documents and acknowledgement receipts.

items.label: 📄 Certificates
items.title: Certificates
body: Income, residence, caste, community, birth, death and disability certificates are foundational documents — and the law specifies clear timelines for issuing them.
bullets: Every certificate request must be acknowledged in writing — keep your receipt.
Most certificates have a maximum issue time defined in the state's Citizen Charter — ask for it.
If a request is denied, you are entitled to a written reason — not silence.

cards.title: Income certificate
cards.description: Usually issued within 7–14 days; supports scholarships, fee waivers and welfare access.

cards.title: Residence certificate
cards.description: Confirms your address with the state; required for school admissions and many welfare schemes.

cards.title: Birth / death certificate
cards.description: Apply within 21 days of the event for routine processing; late registration is allowed but takes longer.

items.label: 🏥 Health
items.title: Health services
body: You are entitled to dignified care at public health facilities — including timely OPD, free essential medicines, and emergency stabilisation regardless of ability to pay.
bullets: Every public hospital should publish its list of free essential medicines.
Emergency care is a right — no facility can deny stabilisation for inability to pay.
You have a right to your own medical records (and increasingly, a portable digital record).

cards.title: Emergency care
cards.description: Right to stabilisation in any hospital, public or private, without upfront payment.

cards.title: Free essential medicines
cards.description: Look for the published list at the OPD counter. Ask for substitutes if a listed medicine is out of stock.

cards.title: Your medical records
cards.description: Right to a copy of your records. In Kerala, eHealth makes them portable across public facilities.

items.label: 🛡 Welfare
items.title: Welfare & pensions
body: Old-age, widow, disability, and other social-security pensions are statutory entitlements when you meet eligibility criteria — not favours.
bullets: Application must be acknowledged in writing; processing timelines are published.
Rejection must come with a reason and an appeal route — not a long silence.
Disbursement dates and amounts are published; mismatches are appealable.

cards.title: Old-age pension
cards.description: Apply through your panchayat or municipality; eligibility usually pegged to age and income.

cards.title: Widow / disability pension
cards.description: Separate statutory schemes with defined eligibility — ask for the form and acknowledge receipt.

cards.title: Track your application
cards.description: Most states publish status online or via the panchayat office. Demand updates if there is silence.

sections.title: What does "good service" actually mean?
body: Good service is not a slogan. It is a set of testable promises — timelines, behaviour, and remedies — that the state publishes and the citizen can hold it to.
Look for Citizen Charters at every government office. If one is missing, that itself is a problem worth raising.
bullets: Promised timeline: how long will this service take?
Required documents: what exactly do you need to bring?
Fees and exemptions: what does it cost, and who is exempt?
Escalation path: if the timeline slips, who do you approach next?

sections.title: The most powerful office near you is the ward sabha
sections.subtitle: Local self-governance is where decisions about your road, school, anganwadi and drainage actually get made. Show up.

items.title: Attend ward sabhas
items.description: Most panchayats hold ward sabhas at least twice a year. Dates are public — your name is on the voter list, so your seat is reserved.

items.title: Submit a proposal
items.description: You can submit written suggestions to the LSGI. A proposal with cost estimates and beneficiary lists travels further than a complaint.

items.title: Volunteer
items.description: Many panchayats welcome volunteers for surveys, audits, school support and disaster drills. Ask the secretary how to register.

sections.title: Step-by-step: raise a grievance and get it closed.
body: Most grievances are resolved at the lowest level when they are raised cleanly. A short, factual complaint with documents attached and a tracking number on file goes faster than the most strongly worded one.
The Oppam model — pioneered in Kerala — is one example of how a district office can close 90%+ of grievances within 96 hours when the process is right.
bullets: Step 1 — Write a one-paragraph factual complaint. Include date, location and what you are asking for.
Step 2 — Submit it (in person / WhatsApp / written / helpline) and get an acknowledgement / tracking ID.
Step 3 — Ask for the name of the assigned officer and the expected timeline.
Step 4 — If timelines slip, escalate to the next level (Tahsildar → Sub-Collector → Collector → State).

items.question: How are certificates issued?
items.answer: You apply (online or at the village office), submit supporting documents, get an acknowledgement, and then either receive the certificate within the published timeline or get a written reason for delay/rejection.

items.question: How do land records work?
items.answer: Each parcel has a survey number, an owner and a history of mutations. The Revenue Department maintains the ownership ledger; the Survey Department maintains the map. Modern systems like ILIMS link the two.

items.question: How do I track my application?
items.answer: Most states publish online status using your acknowledgement number. If there is no online tracker, you are entitled to call the office and ask — and to escalate when you don't hear back.

items.question: What if my grievance is ignored?
items.answer: Escalate. Most departments have a clear escalation chain (junior → senior → district → state). Use it in writing, and reference your earlier tracking ID.

sections.title: Send us your question. We'll point you in the right direction.
sections.subtitle: Surajyapatham is not a government office — but we can help you find the right one, and write your message in a way that gets a faster reply.
